title: Isolation Forest
blurb: Anomalies are few, and they are different. Both of those make them easy to cut off from everything else — and that is the whole algorithm.

title: XGBoost
blurb: Why predict the answer when you can predict your own mistakes? How trees, gradients and shrinkage turn a sequence of simple rules into the default model for tabular data.

title: LightGBM
blurb: Bucket a column into 255 bins and the search for its best split stops being a scan over rows. It costs less than half a percent of the accuracy — and the speed does not come from where almost everyone says it does.

title: K-Means
blurb: Two moves, repeated until nothing changes. The algorithm always stops, it never makes things worse, and it is under no obligation whatsoever to be right.

title: Autoencoders
blurb: Squeeze data through a narrow layer and ask for it back, and a linear autoencoder rediscovers principal component analysis — in a basis nobody asked for, which it will never fix, because nothing in the loss can tell the difference.

title: Shapley Values
blurb: Three people, one fee, and no obvious way to split it. The answer game theory settled in 1953 turns out to be the answer to a question nobody was asking then: what did each feature contribute to this prediction?

title: SMOTE
blurb: The whole algorithm is one line: put a new minority point somewhere on the segment between two old ones. That line is a claim about the space between — where the claim is false, and what it was buying you anyway.

title: F1 Score
blurb: Maximising F1 on a validation set is the standard way to pick a classification threshold. The rule has a closed form, it is not about your problem, and it asserts a cost ratio nobody chose.

title: DBSCAN & HDBSCAN
blurb: Every value of eps you could try is one horizontal line drawn across the same tree. When the branches do not line up, none of them is right — not a hard search, an empty set — and HDBSCAN's answer is to stop cutting straight.

title: Population Stability Index
blurb: Every reading is how far the population moved plus (B−1)(1/N + 1/M), and the second term is there whether anything moved or not. The 0.10 and 0.25 lines ignore it — so on a small segment the traffic light is mostly reporting your sample size, and on a large one it cannot see a shift worth eight points of approval rate.

title: Constrained choice
blurb: A pay rise makes free time dearer and makes you richer, and every course says theory cannot tell you which effect wins. For the utility function every course draws it does: they cancel to the last digit the arithmetic can carry, at every wage — and what actually shortened the working day was a subsistence floor getting out of the way, not one effect beating the other.

title: Nash equilibrium
blurb: One game in eight has no equilibrium you can find by checking cells. In those games your own behaviour is built entirely from the other player's payoffs — so raising a penalty does not reduce the thing it punishes, it buys less monitoring, at exactly the rate that leaves misconduct where it was.

title: Comparative advantage
blurb: Two economies both gain at any price between their opportunity costs, but nobody gets to choose the price. Relative size sets it, both gain only inside a band exactly as wide as the gap between their costs, and an economy that is better at everything, trading with a partner its own size, can come away with exactly nothing.
